claim: Spinosad is an 85%:15% mixture of spinosyns A and D, natural fermentation products of the soil bacterium Saccharopolyspora spinosa.
source: Spinosad is an 85%:15% mixture of spinosyns A and D, natural fermentation products of the soil bacterium Saccharopolyspora spinosa.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript as a factual description of spinosad's composition and origin.

claim: Spinosad occupies a small (3%) but growing share of the global insecticide market.
source: It occupies a small (3%) but growing share of the global insecticide market (Sparks et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sparks et al., 2017.

claim: Spinosad is registered for use in more than 80 countries and applied to over 200 crops to control numerous pest insects.
source: It is registered for use in more than 80 countries and applied to over 200 crops to control numerous pest insects (Biondi et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Biondi et al., 2012.

claim: Recommended dose rates for spinosad vary greatly depending on the pest and crop, ranging from 96 parts per million (ppm) for Brassica crops to 480 ppm in apple fields.

claim: Spinosad targets the highly conserved nAChRα6 subunit of nAChRs in Drosophila melanogaster and a range of other insect species.
source: Studies using mutants, field-derived-resistant strains, and heterologous expression have shown that spinosad targets the highly conserved nAChRα6 subunit of nAChRs in Drosophila melanogaster (hereafter Dα6) and a range of other insect species (Perry et al., 2015; Perry et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Perry et al., 2015 and Perry et al., 2007.

claim: Spinosad is an allosteric modulator, binding to a site in the C terminal region of the nAChRα6 protein.
source: Spinosad is an allosteric modulator, binding to a site in the C terminal region of the protein (Puinean et al., 2013; Somers et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Puinean et al., 2013 and Somers et al., 2015.

claim: Salgado and Saar, 2004 found that spinosad allosterically activates non-desensitized nAChRs, but that low doses were also capable of antagonizing the desensitized nAChRs.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Salgado and Saar, 2004.

claim: It is currently accepted that spinosad causes an increased sensitivity to ACh in certain nAChRs and an enhanced response at some GABAergic synapses, causing involuntary muscle contractions, paralysis, and death.

claim: Both acute and chronic exposures to spinosad cause Dα6 protein levels in the larval brain to decrease.
